title: Networking Fundamentals: How a Request Reaches Your App
subtitle: Understand IP addresses, subnets, routes, DNS, ports and security groups before deploying a container.
analogy: A subnet is a neighborhood, a route table is its road map, and a security group is a door policy. A road to a building does not mean its door is open.
objectives: Explain CIDR ranges, ports, routing and stateful firewalls.
Build public and private subnets across two Availability Zones.
Trace inbound HTTP separately from outbound internet access.
Diagnose routing and security-group failures independently.
prerequisites: AWS CLI v2 authenticated to a learning account; choose us-east-1 for consistency with examples.

lessons.title: IP addresses, CIDR and ports
body: `10.42.0.0/16` is a private IPv4 range. A `/24` subnet holds a smaller part of it; subnets in one VPC cannot overlap. Ports select listening processes: our API listens on 8000, PostgreSQL on 5432, and Redis-compatible services on 6379.

A URL first resolves through DNS. TCP must reach the destination port before HTTP can work. A timeout usually points to reachability; a connection refusal often means no listener; an HTTP 5xx means some HTTP server answered.

lessons.title: What makes a subnet public?
body: A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway. A private subnet does not. A private IPv4 workload can use a NAT gateway for outbound internet access. Put the NAT gateway in a public subnet with an Elastic IP, and point the private default route to it.

A public subnet alone does not give an EC2 instance a public IP. Private tasks can still receive ALB traffic because both endpoints have private VPC connectivity. NAT is not on the ALB-to-task request path.

lessons.title: Security groups and routes solve different problems
body: Routes select a next hop. Security groups permit traffic to an attached network interface; their rules are stateful, so response traffic to allowed connections is permitted. Network ACLs operate at the subnet boundary and are stateless.

Allow public HTTP only to the lab ALB; allow API port 8000 only from the ALB security group; allow data ports only from the app security group. A source security group is a reference to interfaces with that group, not a blanket IP range.

lessons.title: Availability and cost
body: Use two public subnets for the ALB and a multi-AZ database subnet group. The Terraform lab uses one NAT gateway to reduce the number of billed gateways; this creates an AZ dependency and may cause cross-AZ data charges.
A production design may use NAT per AZ and VPC endpoints. Two subnets alone do not make a single database or cache node highly available.

handHoldingSteps: Authenticate with AWS IAM Identity Center using aws configure sso / aws sso login, then confirm account identity before creating anything.
For the optional manual path, create a separate VPC named bootcamp-manual with 10.42.0.0/16. Add public 10.42.0.0/24 and 10.42.1.0/24 plus private 10.42.10.0/24 and 10.42.11.0/24 in two AZs.
Attach an internet gateway. Create a public route table with 0.0.0.0/0 to that gateway. Allocate an Elastic IP and create a NAT gateway in the first public subnet.
Create a private route table with 0.0.0.0/0 to NAT and explicitly associate both private subnets. Keep database and app interfaces private.

Create alb-sg, app-sg and data-sg using the rules described above. Record IDs rather than relying on names, which may exist in multiple VPCs. The Terraform chapter creates a fresh stack; it does not automatically adopt this manual one.
concepts: Routing: The default route applies only when a more specific route does not match.
Stateful security groups: Return traffic for an allowed connection does not require a reverse ingress rule.
Private does not mean offline: NAT and service endpoints can provide outbound access without public workload IPs.

commands.command:
aws configure sso
aws sso login --profile bootcamp
export AWS_PROFILE=bootcamp
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
aws sts get-caller-identity
commands.explanation: Configure a named SSO profile and verify the target account. Use your organization’s start URL and permission set.
commands.expected: The account ID and assumed-role ARN belong to the intended learning account.

commands.command:
aws ec2 describe-vpcs --query 'Vpcs[*].[VpcId,CidrBlock]' --output json
aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=VPC_ID --output json
commands.explanation: Replace VPC_ID with your VPC ID. Read-only discovery helps verify subnet placement.
commands.expected: Four intended subnet CIDRs in the chosen VPC.

commands.command:
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=VPC_ID --output json
aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=VPC_ID --output json
commands.explanation: Inspect actual route associations and group rules rather than guessing from names.
commands.expected: Public default routes use IGW; private default routes use NAT.

codeFiles.code:
Internet -> ALB : TCP 80 (lab only; HTTPS for real users)
ALB security group -> app security group : TCP 8000
App security group -> data security group : TCP 5432 and 6379
Private task -> NAT -> Internet : outbound image/API access
No direct Internet -> database or cache path

breakItDrill.title: Remove an app ingress rule
breakItDrill.scenario: Remove the ALB-source rule on port 8000 in the manual lab.
breakItDrill.symptom: The ALB can be reachable while targets fail health checks.
breakItDrill.fix: Restore only the ALB security group as source; do not expose 8000 to the entire internet.

assignment.title: Draw the two traffic paths
assignment.description: Explain inbound client → ALB → API and outbound API → NAT → internet. Label subnet boundaries, security groups and ports.
assignment.completionHint: Verify the result yourself, then complete the chapter checklist.

recallNote.keyTakeaway: Routing creates a path; a security group permits a connection on that path.
bullets: A NAT gateway is for outbound IPv4 access, not inbound ALB requests.
The ALB uses public subnets; tasks and data stay private.
One NAT and one database node are learning simplifications.
